lesson.title: Beyond the Percentage: Interpreting R-Squared Correctly
lesson.summary: R-squared must be interpreted in the context of the two variables being studied, and a high value does not by itself prove a line is the right model or that anything predicted will be accurate.
lesson.body:
Calculating r-squared is only half the job; stating what it means, in context, in a single well-formed sentence, is the skill that AP Statistics actually rewards. The correct template is: "About [r-squared as a percent] of the variation in [response variable] is explained by the linear relationship with [explanatory variable]." Using the study-hours example, where r-squared = 0.9923, the interpretation is: about 99.2% of the variation in exam scores among these students is explained by the linear relationship with hours studied. Notice everything that sentence includes: the percentage, the response variable by name, the explanatory variable by name, and the word "linear," since r-squared specifically measures how well a straight line fits, not how well any relationship at all fits.

A common mistake is to say r-squared tells you "how accurate the predictions are" or "the percentage of points the line gets right." Both are wrong. R-squared is about variation, not accuracy of individual predictions, and no points are being "gotten right" or "wrong" in a pass-fail sense; every point contributes some squared residual, large or small, to the calculation. Another common mistake is treating r-squared as if it applies to x causing y. An r-squared of 0.9923 says the linear relationship between hours studied and score explains almost all the variation in this small data set; it says nothing about whether studying more hours actually causes higher scores, since correlation and even a strong linear fit never establish causation on their own. Two data sets can also share the exact same r-squared while representing very different practical situations, so the number should always be reported alongside the actual regression equation and a look at the scatterplot, never in isolation.

It is also a mistake to treat a high r-squared as proof that a linear model was the right choice. Recall the y = x-squared example from residual analysis: fitting a straight line to (1,1), (2,4), (3,9), (4,16), (5,25) can still produce a fairly high r-squared over a limited range of x, even though the residual plot clearly showed a U-shaped curve proving the relationship is not actually linear. R-squared summarizes overall fit as a single number; it cannot show you the U-shape hiding inside that number the way a residual plot can. That is why the two tools are used together: the residual plot checks whether a line is the right shape of model, and r-squared, once you are confident the shape is right, tells you how much of the variation that line accounts for.

Finally, r-squared is sensitive to the specific sample it was calculated from. A single unusual point, especially one with an extreme x-value, can inflate or deflate r-squared substantially, a concern that becomes central when studying influential points. For now, the key habit to build is this: whenever you report r-squared, name both variables, say "linear relationship," and never claim more than the number actually supports.
